claim: To inspect and edit interior geometry inside an enclosed hollow shape without hiding objects in the Outliner or permanently changing visibility, use the viewport Clipping Border (Alt+B) to draw a temporary cross-section box that exposes the inner cavity wall -- work directly on the exposed interior, then Alt+B again to clear the clip and restore the normal view.
supporting_evidence: Gemini video-understanding observation (2026-08-14, watched full video): at 15:32-15:52, a hollow robot head's inner cavity wall is exposed via Alt+B clipping border, edited with an inset extrusion, then the clip is cleared with Alt+B again.
rejected_alternative: Hiding outer geometry in the Outliner to reach the interior

claim: Standard Edge Slide (G, G) stops at an open mesh boundary edge; holding Alt (or pressing C) during the slide disables clamping and projects the slide beyond the original boundary along the exact angle of the adjacent faces -- useful for extending a tapered/conical open form (a funnel, bottle neck, nozzle) without disturbing its existing slope.
supporting_evidence: Gemini video-understanding observation: at 31:10-31:30, an unclamped edge slide (Alt held) on a tapered funnel's open boundary extends its length along the existing conical angle, beyond where a normal clamped slide would stop.
rejected_alternative: Manually scaling/recalculating the angle to extend a tapered open form

claim: To close a circular open boundary (an even vertex count around the rim) with clean quad topology instead of a single large n-gon or a triangle-fan pole: use Ctrl+F > Grid Fill instead of a plain F fill -- Grid Fill generates a uniform quad grid across the opening with adjustable Span/Offset parameters, avoiding the center-pinching artifact a large n-gon cap produces under Subdivision Surface.
supporting_evidence: Gemini video-understanding observation: at 37:40-37:55, an open cylinder top with an even vertex count is capped via Ctrl+F Grid Fill instead of a plain F n-gon fill, producing a uniform quad grid.
rejected_alternative: Filling the open boundary with a single n-gon face (F)
reason: A single large n-gon cap pinches at its center under Subdivision Surface; Grid Fill's quad grid distributes the geometry evenly instead.

claim: To slide a multi-vertex selection (e.g. a collar/ring detail) cleanly along an arbitrarily-angled pipe or surface without shearing/distorting it (which happens under normal Local/Global transform orientation), set Transform Orientation to 'Normal' and Pivot Point to 'Active Element' with one representative face on the detail selected as the active element -- this aligns the transform gizmo's axis to that face's normal, so a drag follows the pipe's actual angle instead of a world/local axis.
supporting_evidence: Gemini video-understanding observation: at 50:33-51:18, a collar ring on an arbitrarily-angled pipe distorts under normal transforms; setting Transform Orientation to Normal and Pivot Point to Active Element aligns the gizmo to a reference face so the ring slides cleanly along the pipe's actual angle.
rejected_alternative: Sliding the detail using standard Global or Local transform orientation
reason: Global/Local transform axes don't follow an arbitrarily-rotated pipe's own angle, causing shearing; a Normal-oriented, active-element-pivoted transform follows the surface's actual direction instead.

claim: To get crisp, hard-surface-quality SubD edges without adding dense manual proximity support loops: set the Bevel modifier's Limit Method to 'Weight', assign Mean Bevel Weight 1.0 and Mean Crease 1.0 to the target edges, and enable both Harden Normals and Auto Smooth -- this combination enforces sharp, clean beveled transitions while keeping the base control cage light and still editable.
supporting_evidence: Gemini video-understanding observation: at 77:24-77:55, pinching/shading artifacts at sharp SubD corners are fixed by setting Bevel Limit Method to Weight, assigning Mean Bevel Weight and Mean Crease of 1.0, and enabling Harden Normals plus Auto Smooth.
rejected_alternative: Adding dense manual support loops around every sharp corner
reason: The weight/crease/harden-normals combination achieves the same crisp-edge result as manual support loops without permanently adding to the base mesh's topology density.

claim: A boolean-cut seam can cause a subsequent Bevel modifier to fail or collapse, because the boolean generates microscopic vertex overlaps/sliver faces along the cut line that break the bevel's limit calculations. Fix: add a Weld modifier between the Boolean and Bevel modifiers in the stack, set to a small merge-distance threshold -- this cleans up the near-duplicate boolean vertices before the Bevel modifier evaluates, restoring a clean chamfer along the seam.
supporting_evidence: Gemini video-understanding observation: at 79:08-79:55, a Bevel modifier fails/collapses along a boolean-cut seam due to microscopic vertex overlaps; adding a Weld modifier (small threshold) between Boolean and Bevel in the stack restores the bevel.
rejected_alternative: Manually cleaning up the boolean's near-duplicate vertices by hand before beveling
reason: A Weld modifier does the same near-duplicate-vertex cleanup procedurally and automatically, positioned exactly where it's needed in the stack, rather than requiring a manual pass every time the boolean changes.

claim: To build a circular pattern of repeated details (gear teeth, radial vents, sprocket wheels, tread patterns) as a flat 2D strip first: model one segment, use an Array modifier (with merge/seam settings enabled) to repeat it along a straight line, then add a Simple Deform modifier set to 'Bend' at 360 degrees around the relevant axis to curl the entire strip into a closed circular ring, finishing with a Weld modifier to merge the seam where the bent ends meet.
supporting_evidence: Gemini video-understanding observation: at 89:00-89:55, a flat gear-tooth strip is repeated with an Array modifier, then bent into a full circular ring with a 360-degree Simple Deform Bend modifier, sealed with a Weld modifier.
rejected_alternative: Manually duplicating and rotating each tooth/detail around a circle
reason: Designing and iterating on the repeating detail is easier on a flat, straight strip than directly on a curved surface; the bend deformation only needs to be applied once at the end.

claim: To make a flat, flexible sheet (a decal, sticker, tape strip, patch) adhere to only part of a curved hull while the rest lifts/curls away freely: add a Shrinkwrap modifier (Project mode) targeting the hull, then in Weight Paint mode paint only the region that should stick (e.g. one edge row) into a vertex group and restrict the Shrinkwrap modifier to that group -- the painted region conforms to the surface while the unpainted region keeps its own independent shape/deformation.
supporting_evidence: Gemini video-understanding observation: at 114:15-115:35, a Shrinkwrap modifier restricted via weight-painted vertex group keeps only the painted top edge row of a curved sheet flush against a hull while the rest curls outward freely.
rejected_alternative: Applying Shrinkwrap to the entire sheet, flattening it completely onto the hull
reason: An unrestricted Shrinkwrap conforms the whole object to the target surface; restricting it via a weight-painted vertex group lets only the intended contact region conform while the rest keeps independent shape/motion.
